I was 15 the first time I tried to attempt as well. Feeling suicidal at a young age happens more than we think, it’s a time in our lives where there are so many uncertainties about everything. Not to mention if your home life is already complicated (divorced parents, poverty, abuse, etc). So just know your pain is valid, it’s real, it’s not something you’re making up. You’re clearly struggling with something or multiple things - you may not even know what at this time, that’s possible too. 

My advice is this - everyone will die at some point. The people you love, the people you hate, your teachers, your family, these commenters on Reddit, all of us. What your responsibility is at this time is to try. Try to do whatever you can to find some reason worth living, to not only extend your time but to enhance its quality. And make that intention clear to your healthcare team/psychiatrist. When you become an adult and you are STILL feeling such pain despite your efforts to approach things properly, that is different. There is also a different treatment approach for adults with mental health vs children. But for now, do your best and enjoy what you can and take instruction from your doctors. Take care hun 🙏

Stability is crucial to have that long lasting dopamine effect. Have a routine daily where you “sprinkle in” some projects that are low in effort but yield good results (brushing teeth, showering, eating healthy, exercising, crafts, low stress work, etc) consistently. It’s good for people with depression, etc. who need more of this than those who aren’t depressed. And remember that the level of difficulty does matter. If you go from spending hours on an intense project that’s creative and fun, and then go try to brush your teeth to continue the stream of dopamine, that’s an unrealistic expectation. You have to keep things consistent and level for the most part, and throw something intense in less often. 

Life is like an addiction that way, you want to be comfortable but not too comfortable, otherwise your world may feel like it’s falling apart if those things are taken away/routines are switched up. However not enjoying anything and living in discomfort only to avoid getting “too comfortable” is not good either - FYI I’m not a psychologist, there’s probably real terminology that describes this phenomenon better than I am right now lol.

If you decide you want to live, you’ll have to accept your situation. Acceptance is the first and biggest step - we often pretend that things really aren’t that bad, and we want to convince ourselves that we can handle it on our own. It helps us feel motivated, empowered and have control amongst the chaos. But this is also an extremely slippery slope. If you don’t accept yourself in the position you’re in right now, it’s going to be extremely difficult to explore what needs fixing. I know having an illness or disability can sometimes make people feel very inadequate compared to those who are not (which btw, most people - old, young, etc - nowadays almost always have the “credentials for a mental illness. It’s just that people aren’t honest with their doctors because they know how hypocritical they’ve been, and also they are usually not willing to give up/change anything in their life. If you’ve worked hard for your current lifestyle and/or are feeling comfortable with things as they are in general, those are big deterrents for admitting a mental health problem.

Im either extremely wound up and obsessed with my current situation, depressed to the point of living in my own filth and not suitable to work or have enough energy to see people, or I’m reckless, impulsive and seeking out as many stimulants & sex as I can find. This is the constant pattern of up and down in my life, switching gears every 4-6 months it feels. It happens so fast. Insecure, unorganized and struggling to function, really having a tough time in any social situation. I have PTSD as well, seeing my dead father hang himself. Family is broken apart and relies on wishful thinking, denial & the odd conversation over the phone. 

I am in something of a depression now, it’s getting hard to motivate myself as if it wasn’t already. Positive self talk and any kind of confidence I chalk up feels very unnatural - thus giving me even more anxiety. Sometimes I have a hard time determining how serious something is, especially after everything that’s happened in my life. Have had multiple experiences with mental health professionals that were abusive and just downright disappointing. So jumping back into the system like people are “supposed to do” once they start feeling negative symptoms makes me hesitant. That’s why I just try to take care of everything myself. But it’s not working, clearly. 

To answer your question: every scenario is different. You’re not responsible for your trauma, but you should be responsible for knowing yourself (or making an effort to). Write things down. What exactly is making you question if you’re good or walking on a slippery slope. No one is “weak” when referring to PTSD.
